Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le |x - y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

derivations.claim: Continuity and attainment in [F2] show that $S_+\cup S_-$ is nonempty and compact: the maximum of $|e|$ is attained and $E>0$, while each level set is closed in the compact interval [F1]. If one of $S_+$ or $S_-$ is empty, take $h=1$ or $h=-1$ according to the sign of the nonempty set; this has degree zero and the required sign.

Suppose both sets are nonempty. Their product is a closed bounded subset of $\mathbb R^2$. For $(x,y),(x',y')\in\mathbb R^2$, the reverse and ordinary triangle inequalities in [F3] give $\bigl||x-y|-|x'-y'|\bigr|\le |(x-y)-(x'-y')|\le |x-x'|+|y-y'|\le2\|(x,y)-(x',y')\|_2$, so the distance function is continuous. By [F2] it attains a minimum separation $\delta=\min\{|x-y|:x\in S_+,\,y\in S_-\}$. This minimum is positive because a minimizing pair at distance zero would give a point in both disjoint sets. Starting at the leftmost point of $S_+\cup S_-$, repeatedly take the first point of the opposite-sign set to the right and the last current-sign point before it. These extrema exist because the level sets are compact, and each transition gives an open gap of length at least $\delta$ containing no point of $S_+\cup S_-$. The gaps are pairwise disjoint subintervals of $[a,b]$, so any $k$ transitions satisfy $k\delta\le b-a$; hence there are finitely many transitions, each with a distinct ordered gap.

If there were at least $n+1$ transitions, choosing one extremal point from each successive sign run would give $n+2$ ordered alternating points, contrary to the hypothesis. Thus the number $k$ of transitions is at most $n$. Choose one point $\xi_j$ in each transition gap and set $h(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^{k}(x-\xi_j)$, where $c\in\{-1,1\}$ is chosen so that $h$ has the sign of $e$ on the first run. The polynomial has degree $k\le n$, has no zero on $S_+\cup S_-$, and changes sign exactly when the extremal sign changes. Hence $e(x)h(x)>0$ on the entire extremal set.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

Therefore $(1,0),(x,0),\ldots,(x^n,0),(0,1)$ is a basis of the domain, while the standard coordinate vectors form a basis of the codomain; both dimensions are $n+2$. 2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by

   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity

$$L_j(x):=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{x-t_k}{t_j-t_k}.$$

$$p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}p(t_j)L_j(x).$$

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\in\mathbb N_0$, and let
$f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$ with $w(x)>0$ for every $x\in I$. A normalized
reduced pair is a pair of real polynomials $p,q$ such that $q>0$ on $I$,
$\deg p\le m$, $\deg q\le n$, $p$ and $q$ have no nonconstant common
divisor, and
$$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}:=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_j^2\right)^{1/2}=1\quad\text{when }q(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_jx^j.$$
The zero rational function is represented by $(p,q)=(0,1)$. By
[[lem-na-reduced-rational-representation-unique]], each rational function
admissible under these conditions has exactly one normalized reduced pair.
Define
$$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I):=\{p/q:(p,q)\text{ is a normalized reduced pair}\}$$
and
$$E_{m,n}(f,w;I):=\inf_{r\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)}\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}.$$
The family is nonempty because it contains $r=0$. For each admissible $r=p/q$,
$q>0$ on $I$ makes $r$ continuous by
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $w(f-r)$ is continuous and bounded
on compact $I$. The infimum is therefore finite, bounded below by zero, and
exists as a real number by completeness of $\mathbb R$.

For $r=p/q\ne0$ in reduced form, put
$$d_{m,n}(r):=\min\{m-\deg p,\ n-\deg q\},\qquad N_{m,n}(r):=m+n-d_{m,n}(r).$$
For $r=0$, define $d_{m,n}(0):=n$ and hence $N_{m,n}(0):=m$. The integer
$d_{m,n}(r)$ is the defect. A candidate is **normal** when $d_{m,n}(r)=0$
and **defective** when $d_{m,n}(r)>0$. The alternation count associated with
the candidate is $N_{m,n}(r)+2$; it equals $m+n+2$ only in the normal case.

Let $F$ be a field and let $f,g\in F[x]$ be not both zero. Repeated polynomial division terminates at a last nonzero remainder, whose monic associate is $d=\gcd(f,g)$. There are $A,B\in F[x]$ such that

$$ Af+Bg=d. $$

Moreover, $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, and every common divisor of $f$ and $g$ divides $d$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

If $R$ is an integral domain and $f,g\in R[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg\ne0$ and

$$ \deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg)=\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g). $$

A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

derivations.claim: Define $\Phi:\mathcal P_m\times\mathcal P_n\to\mathbb R[x]$ by $\Phi(u,v)=uq-pv$. It is linear. If $r=0$, [F1] gives $p=0,q=1,d=n,N=m$, so $\Phi(u,v)=u$ and its image is exactly $\mathcal P_m=\mathcal P_N$.

Suppose $r\ne0$. If $(u,v)\in\ker\Phi$, then $uq=pv$. Multiply the Bézout identity in [F2] by $u$: $u=Apu+Bqu=Apu+Bpv=p(Au+Bv)$, so $u=hp$ for $h:=Au+Bv$. Substitution into $uq=pv$ and cancellation of the nonzero polynomial $p$ give $v=hq$. Conversely, every $(hp,hq)$ lies in the kernel.

The degree bounds on $u=hp$ and $v=hq$, together with [F4], are equivalent to $\deg h\le\min(m-\deg p,n-\deg q)=d$; the zero polynomial $h$ is included. Thus the kernel has basis $(p,q),(xp,xq),\ldots,(x^dp,x^dq)$ and dimension $d+1$. By [F3] and [F5], the image dimension is $(m+n+2)-(d+1)=m+n+1-d=N+1$.

For all $u,v$, the degree of $uq-pv$ is at most $\max(m+\deg q,n+\deg p)=m+n-d=N$ by [F1] and [F4]. Hence the image is a subspace of $\mathcal P_N$, whose dimension is $N+1$ by [F5]. Its dimension from step 3.1 is also $N+1$, so the two spaces are equal.

nonconstant polynomial divides both entries. We identify $p/q$ and $p'/q'$ as
the same rational function exactly when $pq'=p'q$. Every quotient with
nonzero denominator has a reduced representation, and any two reduced
representations of the same nonzero rational function differ by a common
nonzero real scalar. The zero rational function has reduced pair $(0,1)$ up to

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

If $p(x)=\sum_{k<n}a_kx^k$ and $p(a)=0$, then there is a real polynomial $q$ with $p(x)=(x-a)q(x)$ for every real $x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-power-difference-factorisation]], [[lem-finite-sum-laws]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field with its order and
absolute value ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[lem-of-abs-value]]), and
neighbourhoods are those of [[def-neighbourhood-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then
$f$ is **continuous at $c$** when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the
language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ with

$$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$

$f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**The point $c$ is required to lie in $A$, and the condition is unpunctured.**
Both differ from [[def-function-limit]], and deliberately. There the quantifier
runs over $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, which removes $x = c$; here $x = c$ is allowed,
and at $x = c$ the implication reads $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$, which is
automatic. So allowing $x = c$ costs nothing, and it is what lets the definition
be stated at every point of $A$, including the points where no limit exists.

**Three clauses, and all three are part of the definition.**

1. **At a limit point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is a limit point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]). Then $f$ is continuous at $c$ if and only if the
   limit of $f$ at $c$ exists and
   $$\lim_{x \to c} f(x) \;=\; f(c)$$
   ([[def-function-limit]]). Indeed, for a given $\varepsilon > 0$ a $\delta$
   witnessing continuity witnesses the limit condition, because the limit
   condition quantifies over a subset of the points continuity quantifies over;
   and conversely a $\delta$ witnessing $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ witnesses
   continuity, because the one point it omits, $x = c$, satisfies
   $|f(c) - f(c)| < \varepsilon$ anyway.

2. **At an isolated point.** Suppose $c \in A$ is an isolated point of $A$
   ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so that $N_{\eta}(c) \cap A = \{c\}$ for some real
   $\eta > 0$. Then **every** $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous at $c$: take
   $\delta := \eta$, so that the only $x \in A$ with $|x - c| < \delta$ is $c$
   itself, and $|f(c) - f(c)| = 0 < \varepsilon$.

3. **On a set.** Continuity on $A$ is continuity at each point of $A$, and
   nothing more. It is not a condition relating $f$ to points outside $A$.

Every point of $A$ is either a limit point of $A$ or an isolated point of $A$,
and never both ([[def-limit-point-r]]), so clauses 1 and 2 between them describe
continuity at every point of $A$.

**This is not the raw $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula of
[[fs-limit-unique-at-every-point-of-the-domain]].** That item records what goes
wrong when the *punctured* formula of [[def-function-limit]] is written down at
an arbitrary point of the domain: at an isolated point it is satisfied
vacuously by every real $L$ at once, so it defines nothing, and this library
therefore leaves $\lim_{x \to c} f(x)$ **undefined** at an isolated point.
Continuity at an isolated point is a different matter: the formula above is not
vacuous — it is a genuine condition on $f(c)$, satisfied because $f(c)$ is the
only value being compared with itself — and it names a single, well-defined
property. The limit is undefined there; the continuity is defined, and is
automatic. Clause 1 is the only place where the two notions meet, and it is
stated only where the limit exists as a notion.

**Where the distinction disappears.** If $A$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-open-and-closed-in-r]]), then every $c \in A$ has some
$N_{\eta}(c) \subseteq A$, and a punctured neighbourhood is never empty
([[def-neighbourhood-r]]), so every point of $A$ is a limit point of $A$ and
clause 1 covers the whole of $A$. The same holds when $A$ is a nondegenerate
interval ([[def-interval]]). Isolated points are what force clause 2 to exist at
all, and they occur as soon as $A$ is allowed to be an arbitrary subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, as in $A = \{0\} \cup [1,2]$.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $t_0,\ldots,t_n$ be distinct real numbers. For
$0\le j\le n$, define
$$L_j(x):=\prod_{k\ne j}\frac{x-t_k}{t_j-t_k}.$$
If $p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}c_kx^k$ has degree at most $n$, then
$$p(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}p(t_j)L_j(x).$$
Consequently, writing $L_j(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\ell_{jk}x^k$, every coefficient
satisfies
$$|c_k|\le\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}|\ell_{jk}|\right)\max_{0\le j\le n}|p(t_j)|.$$
The empty product convention gives $L_0=1$ when $n=0$.

If $R$ is an integral domain and $f,g\in R[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg\ne0$ and

$$ \deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg)=\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g). $$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

derivations.claim: Let $\gamma:=\min_{x\in I}w(x)>0$ and $M:=\|wf\|_{\infty,I}$. Positivity of $\gamma$ follows because the continuous positive function $w$ attains its minimum on compact $I$ by [F3]. In the coefficient space for pairs $(p,q)$ of degrees at most $(m,n)$ and an extra scalar $t$, define $K$ by $\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}=1$, $q(x)\ge0$ on $I$, $0\le t\le M$, and $|w(x)(f(x)q(x)-p(x))|\le t q(x)$ for every $x\in I$. The triple $(0,1,M)$ lies in $K$, so $K$ is nonempty.

The coefficient norm equation, the interval for $t$, and each pointwise inequality defining $K$ are closed conditions on the finite coefficient vector, so $K$ is closed. Its denominator coefficients have norm $1$, and for every $(p,q,t)\in K$, $|p(x)|\le(|f(x)|+M/\gamma)q(x)$ on $I$. real-valued continuous functions on $I$. For $h\in C(I,\mathbb R)$ set
$\|h\|_{\infty,I}:=\sup_{x\in I}|h(x)|$. For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, let
$\mathcal P_n(I)$ be the restrictions to $I$ of real polynomials of degree at
most $n$, including the zero polynomial, and define
$$E_n(f;I):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n(I)}\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}.$$
When $I=[-1,1]$, this agrees with the published definition
[[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]].

These quantities are finite and well-defined. The interval is compact by
[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]], so each
continuous difference $f-p$ has a finite maximum absolute value. The
polynomial space contains $0$, hence the set of errors is nonempty and bounded
below by $0$; completeness of $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) supplies its infimum.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $e:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$E=\|e\|_{\infty,I}>0$. Put
$S_+=\{x\in I:e(x)=E\}$ and $S_-=\{x\in I:e(x)=-E\}$. If there are no
$n+2$ increasing points of $S_+\cup S_-$ with alternating signs, then there
is a real polynomial $h$ of degree at most $n$ such that
$e(x)h(x)>0$ for every $x\in S_+\cup S_-$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

A **formal real polynomial** is either the zero polynomial $0$, or a finite coefficient list $(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$ with $a_n\ne0$; we write the latter as $p(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kX^k$. The list, rather than the function it induces, is the polynomial object. Its **evaluation** at $x\in\mathbb R$ is the real number $p(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_kx^k$.

For nonzero $p=(a_0,\ldots,a_n)$, define $\deg p:=n$ and $\operatorname{lc}(p):=a_n$. The zero polynomial has no degree and no leading coefficient. A nonzero polynomial is **monic** when $\operatorname{lc}(p)=1$. Thus degree and leading coefficient are defined from the displayed finite list, without asserting that distinct formal polynomials define distinct functions. The conventions for finite sums and integer powers used in the evaluation are recorded in [[def-finite-sum]], [[def-integer-power]].

A nonzero real polynomial of degree $n$ has at most $n$ distinct real roots. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]], [[lem-real-polynomial-factor-at-a-root]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

At each $x_i$, $f(x_i)-r(x_i)$ equals either $E$ or $-E$. It is the average of $f(x_i)-p(x_i)$ and $f(x_i)-q(x_i)$, each lying in $[-E,E]$. An average of two numbers in this interval equals $E$ only if both are $E$, and equals $-E$ only if both are $-E$. Thus $p(x_i)=q(x_i)$ for all $n+2$ nodes.

**Inputs.** A nondegenerate interval $I=[a,b]$, a degree $n\ge0$, a continuous
real function $f$ on $I$, an integer exchange budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and an initial reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n+1})$ with $a\le x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}\le b$. Also supply an
exact extrema oracle for a polynomial candidate $p$. On each call it returns
one of:

- alternation$(E,y_0,\ldots,y_{n+1})$, only when $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and the
  returned ordered distinct nodes lie in $I$ and satisfy
  $f(y_i)-p(y_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE$ for one fixed sign $\sigma$;
- maximum$(E,y)$, only when $y\in I$, $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and
  $|f(y)-p(y)|=E$; or
- inconclusive, when neither exact certificate can be returned.

**Procedure.** For $k=0,\ldots,B$, solve the unique real linear system
$$p_k(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda_k=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1,$$
for $p_k\in\mathcal P_n(I)$ and $\lambda_k\in\mathbb R$, using
[[lem-na-polynomial-remez-system-invertible]]. Query the oracle for $p_k$.
If it returns alternation$(0,Y)$ or maximum$(0,y)$, return exact$(p_k)$,
since either response certifies zero uniform error. If it returns
alternation$(E,Y)$ with $E>0$, return certified$(p_k,E,Y)$; the optimality
claim is discharged by [[thm-na-polynomial-equioscillation-certificate]]. If
it returns inconclusive, return oracle-inconclusive. If it returns
maximum$(E,y)$ with $E>0$ and $E=|\lambda_k|$, return certified$(p_k,E,X)$,
because the solved equations make $X$ an alternating set and the oracle
certifies the global norm. If $\lambda_k=0<E$, return zero-level-no-exchange.

In the remaining case, let $s=\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-p_k(y))$. Find the
smallest index $i$ for which $s=\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_k)(-1)^i$ and
replacing $x_i$ by $y$ preserves a strictly increasing reference tuple under
these tests: for $i=0$, require $a\leq y<x_1$; for $i=n+1$, require
$x_n<y\leq b$; and for $0<i<n+1$, require $x_{i-1}<y<x_{i+1}$. Thus a
global maximum at an endpoint may replace the corresponding endpoint reference
node, while distinctness and strict ordering are retained. Replace $x_i$ by
$y$ and continue. If no such index exists, return
no-order-preserving-exchange. If all $B+1$ iterations finish without a
certificate, return budget-exhausted with the last candidate and reference.

**Outputs.** The procedure returns an exact best-approximation certificate,
an exact zero-error candidate, or one of the explicit inconclusive,
zero-level, no-exchange, or budget statuses. It asserts no convergence of the
iterates. Any implementation must ensure each exact solve and oracle call
terminates.

Let $n\ge0$, let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be any function,
and let $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ be distinct nodes in $I$. There is a unique pair
$(p,\lambda)\in\mathcal P_n(I)\times\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$p(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1.$$

Therefore [F2] supplies a unique solve on every entered iteration, and the termination hypothesis together with [F1] gives a terminating oracle call or one reference update.

The loop indices are exactly $0,\ldots,B$, a finite set of $B+1$ iterations. Each entered iteration makes one linear solve and at most one oracle call, so there are at most $B+1$ solves and $B+1$ oracle calls in total. Each iteration returns or advances once, so after at most $B+1$ iterations the procedure either has returned earlier or returns budget-exhausted.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\in\mathbb N_0$, and let
$f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$ with $w(x)>0$ for every $x\in I$. A normalized
reduced pair is a pair of real polynomials $p,q$ such that $q>0$ on $I$,
$\deg p\le m$, $\deg q\le n$, $p$ and $q$ have no nonconstant common
divisor, and
$$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}:=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_j^2\right)^{1/2}=1\quad\text{when }q(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_jx^j.$$
The zero rational function is represented by $(p,q)=(0,1)$. By
[[lem-na-reduced-rational-representation-unique]], each rational function
admissible under these conditions has exactly one normalized reduced pair.
Define
$$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I):=\{p/q:(p,q)\text{ is a normalized reduced pair}\}$$
and
$$E_{m,n}(f,w;I):=\inf_{r\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)}\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}.$$
The family is nonempty because it contains $r=0$. For each admissible $r=p/q$,
$q>0$ on $I$ makes $r$ continuous by
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $w(f-r)$ is continuous and bounded
on compact $I$. The infimum is therefore finite, bounded below by zero, and
exists as a real number by completeness of $\mathbb R$.

For $r=p/q\ne0$ in reduced form, put
$$d_{m,n}(r):=\min\{m-\deg p,\ n-\deg q\},\qquad N_{m,n}(r):=m+n-d_{m,n}(r).$$
For $r=0$, define $d_{m,n}(0):=n$ and hence $N_{m,n}(0):=m$. The integer
$d_{m,n}(r)$ is the defect. A candidate is **normal** when $d_{m,n}(r)=0$
and **defective** when $d_{m,n}(r)>0$. The alternation count associated with
the candidate is $N_{m,n}(r)+2$; it equals $m+n+2$ only in the normal case.

For $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, $m,n\ge0$, $f\in C(I,\mathbb R)$, and a strictly
positive continuous weight $w$, there is $r_*\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$ such
that
$$\|w(f-r_*)\|_{\infty,I}=E_{m,n}(f,w;I).$$

Let $r=p/q\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$ be nonzero, with its reduced pair and
defect $d=d_{m,n}(r)$, and put $N=m+n-d$. Then
$$\{u q-p v:u\in\mathcal P_m,\ v\in\mathcal P_n\}=\mathcal P_N.$$
For $r=0$ with the convention $p=0,q=1,d=n,N=m$, the same equality holds.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $e:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let
$E=\|e\|_{\infty,I}>0$. Put
$S_+=\{x\in I:e(x)=E\}$ and $S_-=\{x\in I:e(x)=-E\}$. If there are no
$n+2$ increasing points of $S_+\cup S_-$ with alternating signs, then there
is a real polynomial $h$ of degree at most $n$ such that
$e(x)h(x)>0$ for every $x\in S_+\cup S_-$.

Let $N\ge0$ and let $x_0<\cdots<x_{N+1}$ be real nodes. Set
$\omega(t)=\prod_{j=0}^{N+1}(t-x_j)$ and
$w_i=\prod_{j\ne i}(x_i-x_j)$. If $g$ is a real polynomial of degree at most
$N$, then
$$\sum_{i=0}^{N+1}\frac{g(x_i)}{w_i}=0.$$
If, for one fixed $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, the values
$\varepsilon(-1)^i g(x_i)$ are all nonnegative, then $g$ is the zero
polynomial.

Let $n\ge0$, let $p$ be a nonzero real polynomial of degree at most $n$, and
let $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ be real numbers. The values $p(x_i)$ cannot all be
nonzero with alternating signs.

Call a pair $(p,q)$ of real polynomials reduced when $q\ne0$ and no
nonconstant polynomial divides both entries. We identify $p/q$ and $p'/q'$ as
the same rational function exactly when $pq'=p'q$. Every quotient with
nonzero denominator has a reduced representation, and any two reduced
representations of the same nonzero rational function differ by a common
nonzero real scalar. The zero rational function has reduced pair $(0,1)$ up to
a nonzero scalar. For $q(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}q_jx^j$, define
$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}:=(\sum_{j=0}^{d}q_j^2)^{1/2}$, unchanged by
appending zero coefficients. If $I$ is a nonempty interval, two reduced
representations of the same rational function with denominators strictly
positive on $I$ and coefficient norm $1$ are equal.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty. The following are equivalent.

1. $A$ is compact.
2. $A$ is closed and bounded.
3. $A$ is pseudocompact.
4. Every continuous $f:A\to\mathbb{R}$ attains a maximum and a minimum on $A$.

This theorem is a ZF statement. The nonemptiness hypothesis is necessary for condition 4, because the empty image has neither a maximum nor a minimum.

derivations.claim: First suppose $E_r>0$ and that $r$ has $N+2$ alternating weighted extrema. If another admissible $s=p'/q'$ had strictly smaller weighted error, write $e_i=w(x_i)(f(x_i)-r(x_i))=\sigma(-1)^iE_r$ and $e_i'=w(x_i)(f(x_i)-s(x_i))$, so $|e_i'|<E_r$. Then $\sigma(-1)^i w(x_i)(s(x_i)-r(x_i))=E_r-\sigma(-1)^ie_i'>0$. Since $w(x_i)q(x_i)q'(x_i)>0$, the numerator $p'q-pq'$ has nonzero alternating signs at those nodes. It lies in $\mathcal P_N$ by [F3], contradicting [F6]. Thus no rational candidate has smaller weighted error and $r$ is best.

Now suppose $r$ is best with $E:=E_r>0$, and put $e=w(f-r)$. It is continuous by [F8], and [F10] makes $|e|$ attain $E$ on compact $I$, so its active-extrema set is nonempty and compact. If it had no $N+2$ alternating points, [F4] would give a polynomial $g\in\mathcal P_N$ with $e(x)g(x)>0$ on that set. By [F3], choose $u,v$ with $\deg u\le m$, $\deg v\le n$, and $g=uq-pv$.
If the best error is zero, then $w(f-r)=0$ everywhere; since $w>0$, $r=f$ pointwise, so the best rational function is unique.

Since $q>0$ on compact $I$, [F10] gives $q_0=\min_I q>0$. For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, $q+\varepsilon v>0$ on $I$. Reduce $(p+\varepsilon u,q+\varepsilon v)$ by [F7]. Its reduced denominator has no zero on $I$, since it divides $q+\varepsilon v$; it is continuous by [F8] and has constant sign by [F9], so a common sign change makes it positive and a further positive scaling gives coefficient norm $1$. Thus $r_\varepsilon=(p+\varepsilon u)/(q+\varepsilon v)$, as a rational function, is represented by an admissible member of $\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$. Its weighted residual is $e_\varepsilon=e-\varepsilon h_\varepsilon$, where $h_\varepsilon:=wg/[q(q+\varepsilon v)]$. On the active-extrema set, $h_0=wg/q^2$ has the same sign as $e$ and is bounded away from zero. By [F8] and [F10], $h_0$ and $e$ are continuous and bounded; the denominator bound implies $h_\varepsilon\to h_0$ uniformly as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Hence there are a neighborhood $U$ of that set and a constant $c>0$ such that $|e|>E/2$, $e$ and $h_\varepsilon$ have the same sign, and $|h_\varepsilon|\ge c$ on $U$ for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$. Shrink $\varepsilon$ further so $\varepsilon\|h_\varepsilon\|_{\infty,I}<E/2$; then $\varepsilon|h_\varepsilon|<|e|$ on $U$ and $|e_\varepsilon|=|e|-\varepsilon|h_\varepsilon|\le E-\varepsilon c<E$. The compact complement $I\setminus U$, if nonempty, contains no active extremum, so [F10] gives $|e|\le E-\eta$ there for some $\eta>0$; a further small choice of $\varepsilon$ makes $\varepsilon\|h_\varepsilon\|_{\infty,I}<\eta/2$. Hence $\|e_\varepsilon\|_{\infty,I}<E$, contradicting best approximation. This proves necessity.

Suppose the best error $E$ is positive and $r,s=p'/q'$ are both best. By step 1.2, $r$ has $N+2$ alternating nodes. At each such node, $w(s-r)=e_r-e_s$ has weak sign $\sigma(-1)^i$, because $|e_s|\le E$. The numerator $g=p'q-pq'$ lies in $\mathcal P_N$ by [F3], and its values have the same weak alternating signs since $wqq'>0$. Thus $\varepsilon(-1)^i g(x_i)\ge0$ with $\varepsilon=\sigma$, so [F5] gives $g=0$ and hence $r=s$.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 prove the two directions of the criterion for positive error; steps 1.3 and 2.2 prove uniqueness in the zero- and positive-error cases. Existence is [F2].

**Inputs.** A nondegenerate interval $I=[a,b]$, degrees $m,n\ge0$, continuous
real target $f$, strictly positive continuous weight $w$, a finite exchange
integer budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, an initial reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{m+n+1})$ satisfying
$a\leq x_0<\cdots<x_{m+n+1}\leq b$, an
exact rational alternation-solver procedure, and an exact weighted-extrema
oracle.

The alternation solver is an explicit input procedure. On a reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{m+n+1})$, it solves the nonlinear equations
$$w(x_i)\bigl(f(x_i)-p(x_i)/q(x_i)\bigr)=(-1)^i\lambda$$
with $p,q$ coprime, $\deg p\le m$, $\deg q\le n$, $q>0$ on $I$, and
$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}=1$. It reports one of: a unique candidate with
defect $d=0$ and its solved level $\lambda$; an exact defective candidate
with its computed $d>0$ and solved level $\lambda$; singular or nonunique
system; no normal solution; or inconclusive. The procedure does not assume
that this nonlinear solve always succeeds.

The weighted-extrema oracle for a returned candidate $r=p/q$ reports one of:

- alternation$(E,Y)$ only when $E=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}$ and $Y$ consists of
  $N_{m,n}(r)+2$ ordered distinct points in $I$ with weighted residuals
  $\sigma(-1)^iE$;
- maximum$(E,x)$ only when $x\in I$, $E=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}$ and
  $|w(x)(f(x)-r(x))|=E$; or
- inconclusive.

**Procedure.** For $k=0,\ldots,B$, call the alternation solver on the current
reference. Return its singular, no-normal-solution, or inconclusive status
unchanged. If it returns a defective candidate, return
defective$(d,N_{m,n}(r))$ immediately; do not apply the normal
$m+n+2$-point count. For a normal candidate $(r,\lambda)$, query the
weighted-extrema oracle. If it returns inconclusive, return
oracle-inconclusive. A response alternation$(0,Y)$ or maximum$(0,x)$
returns exact$(r)$, since either certifies zero weighted error. An
alternation response with $E>0$ returns certified$(r,E,Y)$, with optimality supplied by
[[thm-na-weighted-rational-alternation-characterization]]. For maximum$(E,x)$
with $E=|\lambda|$, the current reference itself is an exact global
alternation certificate, so return certified$(r,E,X)$. If $\lambda=0<E$,
return zero-level-no-exchange. If $E>|\lambda|$,
exchange the returned maximum point $x$ for the smallest reference node $x_i$
whose expected sign $\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda)(-1)^i$ matches the sign of
$w(x)(f(x)-r(x))$ and for which replacing $x_i$ by $x$ preserves strict
ordering. If no such index exists, return no-valid-exchange. After $B+1$
unsuccessful iterations, return budget-exhausted.

**Outputs.** The procedure returns an exact minimax certificate, an exact
zero-error candidate, or an explicit defect, singularity, no-solution,
oracle, exchange, or budget status. It claims no existence of a successful
nonlinear solve and no iterative convergence.

derivations.claim: Every entered iteration has exactly one solver call; if the solver returns a status, the procedure terminates. If it returns a defective candidate, the explicit defect branch terminates. Otherwise a normal candidate receives one oracle call. An inconclusive response returns oracle-inconclusive; every other response either returns a certificate or zero-level status, or searches the finite reference set for an exchange and then returns no-valid-exchange or updates one node. Thus each iteration terminates under the given termination hypothesis.

The loop has only the indices $0,\ldots,B$, so it has at most $B+1$ iterations. Each iteration makes one solver call and at most one oracle call, giving at most $B+1$ calls to each procedure. If no earlier branch returns, the final iteration is followed by budget-exhausted. Therefore the procedure terminates within the stated total call bound.

Let $n\ge0$, let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $f:I\to\mathbb R$ be any function,
and let $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ be distinct nodes in $I$. There is a unique pair
$(p,\lambda)\in\mathcal P_n(I)\times\mathbb R$ satisfying
$$p(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1.$$

**Inputs.** A nondegenerate interval $I=[a,b]$, a degree $n\ge0$, a continuous
real function $f$ on $I$, an integer exchange budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, and an initial reference
$X=(x_0,\ldots,x_{n+1})$ with $a\le x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}\le b$. Also supply an
exact extrema oracle for a polynomial candidate $p$. On each call it returns
one of:

- alternation$(E,y_0,\ldots,y_{n+1})$, only when $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and the
  returned ordered distinct nodes lie in $I$ and satisfy
  $f(y_i)-p(y_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE$ for one fixed sign $\sigma$;
- maximum$(E,y)$, only when $y\in I$, $E=\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}$ and
  $|f(y)-p(y)|=E$; or
- inconclusive, when neither exact certificate can be returned.

**Procedure.** For $k=0,\ldots,B$, solve the unique real linear system
$$p_k(x_i)+(-1)^i\lambda_k=f(x_i),\qquad 0\le i\le n+1,$$
for $p_k\in\mathcal P_n(I)$ and $\lambda_k\in\mathbb R$, using
[[lem-na-polynomial-remez-system-invertible]]. Query the oracle for $p_k$.
If it returns alternation$(0,Y)$ or maximum$(0,y)$, return exact$(p_k)$,
since either response certifies zero uniform error. If it returns
alternation$(E,Y)$ with $E>0$, return certified$(p_k,E,Y)$; the optimality
claim is discharged by [[thm-na-polynomial-equioscillation-certificate]]. If
it returns inconclusive, return oracle-inconclusive. If it returns
maximum$(E,y)$ with $E>0$ and $E=|\lambda_k|$, return certified$(p_k,E,X)$,
because the solved equations make $X$ an alternating set and the oracle
certifies the global norm. If $\lambda_k=0<E$, return zero-level-no-exchange.

In the remaining case, let $s=\operatorname{sgn}(f(y)-p_k(y))$. Find the
smallest index $i$ for which $s=\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_k)(-1)^i$ and
replacing $x_i$ by $y$ preserves a strictly increasing reference tuple under
these tests: for $i=0$, require $a\leq y<x_1$; for $i=n+1$, require
$x_n<y\leq b$; and for $0<i<n+1$, require $x_{i-1}<y<x_{i+1}$. Thus a
global maximum at an endpoint may replace the corresponding endpoint reference
node, while distinctness and strict ordering are retained. Replace $x_i$ by
$y$ and continue. If no such index exists, return
no-order-preserving-exchange. If all $B+1$ iterations finish without a
certificate, return budget-exhausted with the last candidate and reference.

**Outputs.** The procedure returns an exact best-approximation certificate,
an exact zero-error candidate, or one of the explicit inconclusive,
zero-level, no-exchange, or budget statuses. It asserts no convergence of the
iterates. Any implementation must ensure each exact solve and oracle call
terminates.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with $a<b$, and let
$p\in\mathcal P_n([a,b])$. If $E:=\|f-p\|_{\infty,[a,b]}>0$ and there are
$n+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ in $[a,b]$ and a sign
$\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such
that
$$f(x_i)-p(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE\qquad(0\le i\le n+1),$$
then no polynomial in $\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ has smaller uniform error than
$p$. Thus the displayed residual values are an a posteriori optimality
certificate.

derivations.claim: The equations at $x_0=0,x_1=1$ are $p+\lambda=0$ and $p-\lambda=1$. Adding them gives $2p=1$, so $p=1/2$ and then $\lambda=-1/2$, in agreement with the unique solve [F1].

For every $x\in[-1,1]$, $|x|\in[0,1]$, so $-|1/2|\le |x|-1/2\le1/2$ and the absolute error is at most $1/2$. It equals $1/2$ at $x=0$ and at $x=1$ (also at $x=-1$), so the oracle returns $E=1/2=|\lambda|$. The residuals at $(0,1)$ are $-1/2,1/2$, hence the procedure returns certified$(p,1/2,X)$ by [F2], and [F3] makes $p$ best.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\in\mathbb N_0$, and let
$f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$ with $w(x)>0$ for every $x\in I$. A normalized
reduced pair is a pair of real polynomials $p,q$ such that $q>0$ on $I$,
$\deg p\le m$, $\deg q\le n$, $p$ and $q$ have no nonconstant common
divisor, and
$$\|q\|_{\mathrm{coef},2}:=\left(\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_j^2\right)^{1/2}=1\quad\text{when }q(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}q_jx^j.$$
The zero rational function is represented by $(p,q)=(0,1)$. By
[[lem-na-reduced-rational-representation-unique]], each rational function
admissible under these conditions has exactly one normalized reduced pair.
Define
$$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I):=\{p/q:(p,q)\text{ is a normalized reduced pair}\}$$
and
$$E_{m,n}(f,w;I):=\inf_{r\in\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)}\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}.$$
The family is nonempty because it contains $r=0$. For each admissible $r=p/q$,
$q>0$ on $I$ makes $r$ continuous by
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $w(f-r)$ is continuous and bounded
on compact $I$. The infimum is therefore finite, bounded below by zero, and
exists as a real number by completeness of $\mathbb R$.

For $r=p/q\ne0$ in reduced form, put
$$d_{m,n}(r):=\min\{m-\deg p,\ n-\deg q\},\qquad N_{m,n}(r):=m+n-d_{m,n}(r).$$
For $r=0$, define $d_{m,n}(0):=n$ and hence $N_{m,n}(0):=m$. The integer
$d_{m,n}(r)$ is the defect. A candidate is **normal** when $d_{m,n}(r)=0$
and **defective** when $d_{m,n}(r)>0$. The alternation count associated with
the candidate is $N_{m,n}(r)+2$; it equals $m+n+2$ only in the normal case.

Let $I=[a,b]$ with $a<b$, let $m,n\ge0$, and let $f,w\in C(I,\mathbb R)$
with $w>0$ on $I$. A best rational approximant in
$\mathcal R_{m,n}^+(I)$ exists and is unique. For a candidate $r=p/q$ with
positive weighted error $E_r:=\|w(f-r)\|_{\infty,I}>0$, let
$N=N_{m,n}(r)=m+n-d_{m,n}(r)$. Then $r$ is best if and only if there are
$N+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{N+1}$ in $I$ and
$\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such that
$$w(x_i)(f(x_i)-r(x_i))=\sigma(-1)^iE_r\qquad(0\le i\le N+1).$$
If the best error is $0$, positivity of $w$ forces the unique best function
to be $f$ itself. In the normal case $d=0$ the count is $m+n+2$; for
defective candidates the count is $m+n+2-d$.

derivations.claim: The pair $p=1/2,q=1$ is reduced, has $q>0$, coefficient norm $1$, degrees $(0,0)$, and error $f-r=x^2-1/2$. Since $x^2\in[0,1]$, this residual lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$ and its absolute value reaches $1/2$ exactly at $x=-1,0,1$. The extremal residual signs in order are $+,-,+$.

Here $d=\min(1-0,1-0)=1$, so the defect-sensitive count is $1+1+2-1=3$. By [F2], the three alternating extrema make $r=1/2$ a best type-$(1,1)$ rational approximant. The extremal set is exactly $\{-1,0,1\}$, so there are not four distinct global extrema; the refuted $m+n+2=4$ count fails.

Let $I=[a,b]\subset\mathbb R$ with $a<b$, and let $C(I,\mathbb R)$ denote the
real-valued continuous functions on $I$. For $h\in C(I,\mathbb R)$ set
$\|h\|_{\infty,I}:=\sup_{x\in I}|h(x)|$. For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, let
$\mathcal P_n(I)$ be the restrictions to $I$ of real polynomials of degree at
most $n$, including the zero polynomial, and define
$$E_n(f;I):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n(I)}\|f-p\|_{\infty,I}.$$
When $I=[-1,1]$, this agrees with the published definition
[[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]].

These quantities are finite and well-defined. The interval is compact by
[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]], so each
continuous difference $f-p$ has a finite maximum absolute value. The
polynomial space contains $0$, hence the set of errors is nonempty and bounded
below by $0$; completeness of $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) supplies its infimum.

Let $n\ge0$, let $f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with $a<b$, and let
$p\in\mathcal P_n([a,b])$. If $E:=\|f-p\|_{\infty,[a,b]}>0$ and there are
$n+2$ ordered nodes $x_0<\cdots<x_{n+1}$ in $[a,b]$ and a sign
$\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$ such
that
$$f(x_i)-p(x_i)=\sigma(-1)^iE\qquad(0\le i\le n+1),$$
then no polynomial in $\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ has smaller uniform error than
$p$. Thus the displayed residual values are an a posteriori optimality
certificate.

For every $f\in C([a,b],\mathbb R)$ with $a<b$ and every $n\ge0$, there is
exactly one $p_*\in\mathcal P_n([a,b])$ with
$\|f-p_*\|_{\infty,[a,b]}=E_n(f;[a,b])$.
